title: Ant Colonies: Teamwork in Tiny Bodies
summary: How an ant colony shares its work, uses scent trails to find food, grows food, survives in the desert, and helps the soil.
poll: A team with no boss can still work well.

versions.title: Ants Work Together
versions.text:
Look at the ground. Do you see a line of ants? They are at work.

Ants live in a big group. The group is a colony. Its home is a nest. The nest has lots of tunnels. Most are in the ground.

Each colony has a queen. She lays the eggs. Most ants are workers. The workers are all female. They dig. They care for the young. They guard the nest. They find food. Some ants are male. They have wings.

An ant finds food. It goes home. It leaves a scent on the ground. The scent is a trail. The rest smell it. They walk to the food. Ants touch heads to share news, too.

Ants are strong. One ant can lift much more than its own weight.

Some ants cut bits of leaf. They grow food on the bits. In Saudi Arabia, some ants run on hot sand. They use the sun to find home.

Ants help the land. Their tunnels let in air and rain. They eat dead bugs. The colony is one big team.

Some ants cut bits of leaves. They grow a kind of food on the leaf bits. In Saudi Arabia, some ants run fast on the hot sand. They use the sun to find the way home.

versions.title: Ants: A Team of Tiny Workers
versions.text:
Look closely at the ground on a warm day. You may see a long line of ants marching along. Each ant is small, but together they do big jobs.

Ants live in a large family called a colony. The colony makes its home in a nest. The nest has many tunnels and rooms, and most of them are under the ground. Some colonies hold thousands of ants.

Every colony has a queen. Her job is to lay eggs. Most of the ants are workers. All the workers are female. They dig tunnels, feed the young ants, guard the nest, and find food. A few ants are male. They have wings and live only a short time.

When a worker finds food, it hurries back to the nest. As it walks, it leaves a scent on the ground. This scent makes a trail. Other ants smell the trail and follow it to the food. Ants also touch their feelers together to share news.

Ants are strong for their size. One ant can carry something much heavier than its own body.

Some ants, called leafcutter ants, carry bits of leaves home. They grow a kind of food on the leaves. In Saudi Arabia, some desert ants run across the hot sand. They use the sun to find their way home.

Ants help nature, too. Their tunnels let air and water into the soil. They also clean up dead bugs. No ant is the boss, yet the colony works as one team.

versions.title: Ants: A Team of Tiny Workers
versions.text:
On a warm afternoon, you might spot a long line of ants crossing the ground. Each ant looks tiny and weak. In fact, it belongs to one of the best teams in nature.

Ants live together in a large family called a colony. Their home is a nest with many tunnels and rooms. Most of it is hidden under the ground. A big colony can have thousands or even millions of ants.

The queen is the only ant that lays eggs. Worker ants are all female, and they do almost every other job. They dig tunnels, feed the young, guard the nest, and gather food. The male ants have wings. They live only a short time. They do not do the colony's work.

When a worker finds food, it hurries back to the nest. Along the way, it leaves a special scent on the ground. This scent makes a trail. Other workers smell it and follow it to the food. Ants also share news by touching their feelers, called antennae.

Ants are very strong for their size. One ant can carry a load many times heavier than its own body.

Leafcutter ants carry pieces of leaves home. They grow a kind of fungus on them for food. In Saudi Arabia, some desert ants race across the hot sand in the middle of the day. They use the sun to find their way home.

Ants help nature, too. Their tunnels let air and water into the soil. They also clean up dead insects. No ant is the boss, yet the colony works together as one team.

versions.title: Ant Colonies: Teamwork in Tiny Bodies
versions.text:

Ants live together in a large family called a colony. Most colonies build a nest with many tunnels and rooms, usually under the ground. A small colony may have a few dozen ants, while a giant one can have millions.

The queen is the only ant that lays eggs. Worker ants are all female, and they do almost every other job. They live only a short time, and their main job is to mate with a young queen.

Ants cannot talk, so they share news in other ways. When a worker finds food, it leaves a trail of a special scent called a pheromone on its way home. Other workers smell the trail with their antennae and follow it to the food. Ants also tap antennae when they meet.

Ants are very strong for their size. One ant can carry a load many times heavier than its own body. When a load is too big, several ants cooperate to move it.

Leafcutter ants carry pieces of leaves into their nest. They do not eat the leaves. Instead, they grow a fungus on them, and the fungus becomes their food. In Saudi Arabia, some desert ants hunt in the hottest part of the day. They use the sun to find their way back home.

Ants also help nature. Their tunnels let air and water into the soil, and they clean up dead insects. No ant gives orders, yet the colony works together as one team.

versions.title: Ant Colonies: Teamwork in Tiny Bodies
versions.text:
On a warm afternoon, you might observe a long procession of ants marching steadily across a sidewalk, each one carrying a crumb or hurrying to find another. Every individual ant appears small and fragile. Yet it belongs to one of the most highly organized communities in the natural world, in which thousands of tiny bodies behave almost like a single living organism.

Ants live together in a large family called a colony. Most colonies construct a nest containing numerous tunnels and chambers, usually beneath the ground, although certain species prefer rotting wood or the space underneath stones. A modest colony may contain only a few dozen ants, while an enormous one can include millions of individuals.

The queen is the only ant that lays eggs, and in some species she may survive for many years. Worker ants are all female, and they perform virtually every other responsibility, often changing jobs as they grow older. Younger workers nurse the eggs and the larvae, which are immature ants that resemble tiny white grubs, while older workers excavate tunnels, defend the entrance, or venture outside to collect food. The male ants have wings, but they live only briefly, because their primary purpose is to mate with a young queen.

Because ants cannot speak, they communicate primarily through chemicals and touch. When a worker discovers food, it deposits a trail of a special chemical scent called a pheromone as it returns home. Other workers detect the trail with their sensitive antennae and follow it directly to the meal. As more ants travel the route and add their own scent, the trail grows stronger, so the colony quickly concentrates its effort on the best food.

Ants are remarkably powerful for their size. A single ant can carry a load many times heavier than its own body, and when an object is too large, several ants coordinate their movements in a display of cooperation to transport it together.

Leafcutter ants carry fragments of leaves into their nest, but they do not consume them. Instead, they cultivate a fungus on the chewed leaves, and that fungus becomes the colony's food. In Saudi Arabia, certain desert ants search for food during the hottest part of the day, when fewer predators are active, and they navigate home across the featureless sand by tracking the position of the sun.

Ants also benefit the environment. Their tunnels aerate the soil, allowing air and water to penetrate it. They also remove dead insects. Remarkably, no ant issues orders; instead, each ant follows simple rules, and together their actions produce an efficient team.

versions.title: Ant Colonies: Teamwork in Tiny Bodies
versions.text:
On a warm afternoon, one might observe a lengthy procession of ants marching steadily across a sidewalk, each one transporting a crumb or hurrying purposefully to locate another. Every individual ant appears insignificant and fragile in isolation, yet it belongs to one of the most sophisticated communities found anywhere in the natural world, in which thousands of minuscule bodies behave collectively almost like a single living organism.

Ants inhabit a large, cooperative family known precisely as a colony. Most colonies construct an elaborate nest containing numerous interconnected tunnels and chambers, usually situated beneath the ground, although certain species prefer decaying wood or the sheltered cavities underneath stones. A modest colony may contain only a few dozen ants, whereas an enormous one can include millions of individuals distributed across an extensive underground territory.

The queen functions as the colony's sole egg-laying female, and in certain species she may survive for many years, vastly outliving the workers around her. Worker ants, all of them female, perform virtually every remaining responsibility within the colony, frequently changing occupations as they mature and age. Younger workers nurse the eggs and the larvae, which are immature ants resembling tiny white grubs, while older workers excavate tunnels, defend the nest entrance, or venture outside to gather provisions for the entire community. The male ants possess wings, but they survive only briefly, because their primary biological purpose is simply to mate with a young, newly emerged queen.

Because ants are categorically incapable of speech, they communicate predominantly through chemical signals and direct physical contact. When a worker discovers food, it deposits a trail of a specialized chemical signal called a pheromone as it returns home, and other workers detect this trail using their sensitive antennae and follow it directly to the meal. As additional ants travel the established route and contribute their own scent to it, the chemical signal intensifies considerably, so the entire colony rapidly concentrates its collective effort on the most productive food source while abandoning less rewarding ones.

Ants are remarkably powerful relative to their diminutive size. A single ant can carry a load many times heavier than its own body weight, and when an object proves too massive for one individual alone, several ants coordinate their movements in an impressive demonstration of cooperation in order to transport it together.

Leafcutter ants carry fragments of leaves into their nest, yet they do not actually consume the leaves themselves. Instead, they cultivate a specialized fungus upon the chewed vegetation, and that fungus subsequently becomes the colony's primary nourishment, which effectively makes these insects some of the earliest agricultural specialists in the history of life on Earth. In Saudi Arabia, certain desert-adapted ants forage during the hottest portion of the day, precisely when fewer predators remain active, and they navigate homeward across the featureless sand by continuously monitoring the sun's position in the sky.

Ants also benefit the surrounding environment considerably. Their extensive tunnels aerate the soil, allowing both air and water to penetrate it more readily, and they efficiently eliminate dead insects that might otherwise accumulate on the surface. Remarkably, no single ant ever issues commands to the others; instead, each individual simply follows a set of simple behavioral rules, and together their countless interactions generate an extraordinarily efficient and resilient collective team.

versions.title: Ant Colonies: Teamwork in Tiny Bodies
versions.text:
On a warm afternoon, an observer might notice a lengthy procession of ants marching steadily across a sidewalk, each one transporting a crumb or hurrying purposefully to locate another. Every individual ant appears insignificant and fragile when considered in isolation, yet it belongs to one of the most sophisticated and highly organized communities found anywhere in the natural world, in which thousands upon thousands of minuscule bodies behave collectively almost as though they constituted a single living organism.

Ants inhabit a large, cooperative family unit known precisely as a colony. Most colonies construct an elaborate subterranean nest containing numerous interconnected tunnels and chambers, usually situated beneath the ground's surface, although certain species prefer decaying wood or the sheltered cavities found underneath stones. A modest colony may contain only a few dozen individual ants, whereas an enormous colony can include millions of individuals distributed across an extensive underground territory spanning considerable distances.

The queen functions as the colony's sole egg-laying female, and in certain species she may survive for many years, vastly outliving the comparatively short-lived workers surrounding her throughout the nest. Worker ants, every one of them female, perform virtually every remaining responsibility within the colony's division of labor, frequently changing occupations as they mature and age through successive life stages. Younger workers nurse the eggs and the larvae, which are immature ants resembling tiny white grubs, while older, more experienced workers excavate tunnels, defend the nest's entrance against intruders, or venture outside to gather provisions on behalf of the entire community. The male ants possess functional wings, but they survive only briefly following their emergence, because their sole biological purpose is simply to mate with a young, newly emerged queen before perishing.

Because ants are categorically incapable of vocal speech, they communicate predominantly through chemical signals and direct physical contact between individuals. When a worker discovers a food source, it deposits a trail of a specialized chemical signal called a pheromone as it returns homeward, and other workers subsequently detect this trail using their exquisitely sensitive antennae and follow it directly to the meal in question. As additional ants travel the established route and contribute their own scent to the accumulating trail, the chemical signal intensifies considerably over time, so the entire colony rapidly concentrates its collective effort on the single most productive food source while simultaneously abandoning less rewarding alternatives.

Ants are remarkably powerful relative to their diminutive physical size. A single ant can carry a load many times heavier than its own body weight, and when an object proves too massive for any one individual alone, several ants coordinate their movements with precision in an impressive demonstration of cooperation in order to transport the object together as a unit.

Leafcutter ants carry fragments of leaves into their underground nest, yet they do not actually consume the leaves themselves at all. Instead, they cultivate a specialized fungus upon the chewed, processed vegetation, and that cultivated fungus subsequently becomes the colony's primary source of nourishment, which effectively makes these particular insects some of the earliest agricultural specialists in the entire history of life on Earth. In Saudi Arabia, certain desert-adapted ants forage during the very hottest portion of the day, precisely when fewer predators remain active in the heat, and they navigate homeward across the featureless desert sand by continuously monitoring the sun's changing position in the sky overhead.

Ants also benefit the surrounding environment quite considerably through their constant activity. Their extensive networks of tunnels aerate the soil, allowing both air and water to penetrate it far more readily than compacted ground otherwise would, and they efficiently eliminate dead insects that might otherwise accumulate on the surface and decompose. Remarkably, no single ant within the colony ever issues commands to any other; instead, each individual simply follows a set of simple behavioral rules in response to local conditions, and together their countless small interactions generate an extraordinarily efficient and resilient collective team that functions without any central authority whatsoever.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to keep ants out of a kitchen
How ants live and work together as a team
Why ants are the strongest animals on Earth
How ants sleep in their nest at night
questions.why: Every part of the article tells how ants share jobs, find food, and help the land as one team.

wrong.A: The article never talks about keeping ants out of a kitchen.
wrong.C: The article says ants are strong for their size, but that is only one small part.
wrong.D: The article does not talk about how ants sleep.

questions.stem: Which ant lays the eggs in a colony?
options: The male ants
The worker ants
The queen
Every ant in the nest
questions.why: The article says each colony has a queen, and she lays the eggs.

wrong.A: Male ants have wings, but they do not lay eggs.
wrong.B: Workers dig, guard, and find food. The queen lays the eggs.
wrong.D: Only one ant, the queen, lays the eggs.

questions.stem: How does an ant show other ants the way to food?
options: It leaves a scent trail on the ground
It shouts loudly to them from the place with food
It carries every ant to the food
It draws a map in the sand
questions.why: The article says the ant leaves a scent on the ground, and the others smell the trail and follow it.

wrong.B: Ants cannot shout. They use scent and touch.
wrong.C: The ant does not carry the others. They follow the trail.
wrong.D: The article does not say ants draw maps.

questions.stem: In this article, what does the word colony mean?
options: A long hole or path that goes under the ground
A kind of food ants grow
The smell an ant leaves
A big group of ants that live together
questions.why: The article says ants live in a big group, and the group is called a colony.

wrong.A: A long hole under the ground is a tunnel.
wrong.B: Ants grow food on leaf bits, but that is not a colony.
wrong.C: The smell an ant leaves is a scent.

questions.stem: The article says one ant can lift more than its own weight. What does this show?
options: Ants are the biggest bugs
Ants are very strong for their size
Ants do not need to eat
Ants like to work alone and not with others
questions.why: Lifting something heavier than your own body takes a lot of strength, so ants are strong for how small they are.

wrong.A: The article says ants are small, not big.
wrong.C: The article says ants find food, so they do need to eat.
wrong.D: The article shows ants work as a team, not alone.

questions.stem: What would most likely happen if an ant found food but left no scent?

The queen would go get it
Other ants would have a hard time finding the food
The ant would forget the way home

wrong.B: The queen lays eggs. She does not go out for food.
wrong.D: The article says desert ants use the sun to find home. A scent is for the other ants.

questions.stem: How do ant tunnels help the land?

They keep all the rain far away from plant roots
They make the ground very hard
They scare away all birds

wrong.C: Tunnels make the soil loose, not hard.
wrong.D: The article does not say anything about birds.

options: To tell readers to stay out of the desert

MID.prompt: Explain how ants share information with one another. Use at least two details from the article to support your answer.
checklist: I gave a clear answer to the question.
I supported my answer with at least two details from the article.

MID.modelAnswer: Ants share information mainly through chemical scent and touch instead of sound. When a worker finds food, it leaves a trail of pheromone as it returns home, and other workers detect this scent with their antennae and follow it straight to the meal, which lets the whole colony cooperate to gather food quickly. Ants also tap their antennae together when they meet, which seems to help them share news and work as one coordinated team.

HIGH.prompt: The article claims that a colony can work well even though no ant gives orders. Explain how this is possible, using at least three details from the article.
checklist: I explained the claim in my own words.
I used at least three details from the article as evidence.
I explained how each detail shows the colony working without a leader.
HIGH.modelAnswer: A colony can function well without any ant giving orders because each ant simply reacts to signals and does its own job, and together those actions add up to organized cooperation. For example, a worker that finds food leaves a pheromone trail, and other ants follow that scent without needing to be told, which lets the whole colony find food efficiently. Likewise, when a load is too heavy for one ant, several ants cooperate automatically to carry it together, and worker ants naturally divide into roles such as caring for larvae, digging tunnels, or defending the nest. None of this requires a leader directing traffic; it shows how simple individual behaviors, repeated by thousands of ants, create complex teamwork for the whole colony.
